text: Of all the monsters Odysseus faced on his long way home, none was more terrible than the Cyclops — a one-eyed giant who ate men alive.
His name was Polyphemus, a savage son of the sea-god Poseidon. He lived alone in a cave, herding his sheep, far from the laws of gods and men.
Odysseus and a few of his crew came into that cave, hoping for the welcome owed to guests. Instead the giant rolled a great stone across the mouth, and sealed them inside.
He seized two of the men and devoured them. The Greeks could not begin to move the stone. They needed a trick — and Odysseus was the master of tricks.
So he offered the giant strong, dark wine. Pleased, the Cyclops asked his name. And Odysseus answered: Οὖτις ἐμοί γ᾽ ὄνομα — Nobody is my name.
When the giant sank into a drunken sleep, they heated a great stake of olive-wood until it glowed, and drove it deep into his single eye.
Polyphemus roared in agony. The other giants came running and called, who is hurting you? And he bellowed back: Nobody is killing me. So they shrugged and went away.
At dawn, Odysseus and his men clung beneath the bellies of the great rams, and so slipped past the blinded giant's groping hands and out of the cave.
Safe at sea, Odysseus could not resist shouting back his true name. And the Cyclops prayed to his father Poseidon for revenge — a curse that would shadow the whole journey home.
And so the cleverest of the Greeks escaped the cave of the Cyclops. But the curse of Poseidon would follow Odysseus across every sea, on his long and bitter road toward home.
